doc.title: Sherrie Maricle interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Burden of booking her own groups and rediscovering the drums
summary: Maricle books DIVA, Five Play and the 3-D Jazz Trio herself, often eight hours a day; the shutdown let her practise for hours and love the drums again, with Jami Dauber managing.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: I had a question that I’ve tried to hone down but I haven’t really done it yet, but are there things that you do now, or let’s say up until March, over the years, that took a lot of time and energy and assuming that at some point we get back to normal, you would think twice about actually doing them again because you’ve noticed that your life is easier because you’re not?

Well man, that’s a great question. What I do spend a lot of my time as the sole booker of the DIVA jazz orchestra and my quintet, Five Play. And I’m a co-leader with a new trio called the 3-D Jazz Trio. So I spend ages and endless amounts of hours and weeks and months and years trying to book those groups. Aggressively. I mean that was part of my day job you know, as a band leader without a booking agency. So in the end sometimes I’d be easily eight hours a day, especially booking a tour, even working on a two week tour, and doing all of it mostly myself. I don’t know — and I haven’t done it, except other than we mentioned before trying to re-book some things that were lost, I haven’t been as aggressive to look for dates in support of other dates, and I don’t know if I’ll necessarily go back to that to such an extreme degree. I was very aggressive about it. And it was successful in many cases but that was a lot of hours in the day where I wasn’t really thinking about music, and that was the kind of activity that makes me not like music, or the music business. Like all the things that don’t have to do with playing your instrument and trying to create something beautiful with other musicians, it can be really frustrating to all of us, every freelance performer, you know, if you’re running your own band or business or whatever it’s just man, all the things that don’t have to do directly with your thing and the creative process can be so taxing and really time consuming and really frustrating. So I’m not saying I’m not going to do it but I’m thinking like I have practiced more, I was practicing one day and I was out just sitting at my drums for well over five hours. Now I haven’t done that at all since college. And I couldn’t believe how fast the time flew by. And everyone talks about, not everyone, but some people talk about being in the flow state where you’re just doing that thing that you love so much. And I’m like flying down different YouTube rabbit holes of lessons and learning and checking

things out. And I’m like man, and I’m getting these little goose bumps sometimes when I’m very enthusiastic about something. And that for me was like oh my God this is so great. Like I actually love the drums again. I love the drums so much. Because when you’re the band leader sometimes there’s just so much other stuff going on I, anyway, forget like I love playing the drums and this is what I’ve done since I was eleven years old. So not being distracted by, “Oh no, we don’t have another gig.” “Oh no, we’re going to lose money if we get this bus.” Or, “Oh gosh, how much is the airline overcharge to move the music stands” and blah blah blah blah blah. You know. And I’m very lucky to have the help of Jami Dauber who’s been acting as our band manager and road manager for quite a while. She’s played trumpet in the band like 23 years. And, but jeez, all that stuff being gone, to further answer your question it’s just like oh, here I am back to kind of the core, you know the center of where my musical journey started, and it reminded me that I really do love it in that way.
